newsitem.title: INDIA: India foreign investment inflows $4.0 bn April-Dec.
newsitem.headline: India foreign investment inflows $4.0 bn April-Dec.

text.p: Inflows of foreign investment in India totalled $4.0 billion in April to December last year, up sharply from $2.6 billion for the same period in 1995, Reserve Bank of India governor Chakravarty Rangarajan said on Tuesday.
He said foreign institutional investment (FII) in the eight months more than doubled to $2.3 billion, compared with $1.1 billion in the year-ago period.
Foreign direct investment (FDI) rose to $1.7 billion in the eight months, up from $1.5 billion in the same period of 1995.
Rangarajan told a conference on infrastructure India needed to raise its savings rate from 25 percent of gross domestic product to 28 percent in order accelerate its growth rate.
"We need to have 28 percent plus to achieve a GDP growth of seven to eight percent," he told the "Advantage Maharashtra" conference.
He said, repeating data given in an RBI report released last week, India was likely to show GDP growth of 6.8 percent in 1996/97 (April-March), slowing slightly from 7.1 percent in the previous year.
Rangarajan said India's fiscal deficit will be about five percent of GDP in 1996/97.
"There are problems to reduce it. But the government's objective is to bring it down to four percent," he said.
"As of today India's foreign exchange reserves stood at $19.3 billion after the repayment of India Development Bonds," the central bank governor said.
"This is one indicator of the resilience in the economy," he said.
Referring to the development of the infrastructure industries, and need for foreign investment, Rangarajan called on the government to improve the climate for investors.
"We need transparency and clarity in government policies including a pricing policy," he said.
He said he will recommend setting up regulatory bodies to monitor infrastructure industries.
Ninety percent of investments in the Indian economy were generated domestically, but the 10 percent made from abroad were critical as they provided more efficient management, he said.
